title: Parolee killed by police had long record: Officers say man was looking for lethal drug dose
article: A man shot and killed by police during an attempted robbery and hostage taking at a downtown pharmacy had a long history of violence and criminal behaviour.
Arthur George Provencal, 34, was on statutory release from Drumheller Institution, where he was serving a federal sentence for armed robbery, the Herald has learned.
Details of his most recent crime and the length of sentence are not known.
However, sources say Provencal had been released from prison last fall and was reporting to a parole officer in Calgary.
Provencal, originally from Ontario, had conflicts with the law from a young age.
In 1987, he was charged with attempted murder following a knife attack in Ottawa, according to reports published in the Ottawa Citizen.
Those charges were reduced when Provencal, then 21, pleaded guilty to assault and was handed a 20-month jail sentence.
Donald Hebert, who was 18 at the time, was attacked and stabbed when he was confronted by two men and a woman after leaving a Halloween party in downtown Ottawa.
Provencal's last attempt at crime unfolded at about 6 p.m. Saturday at the Shoppers Drug Mart on the second floor of Toronto Dominion Square
The mall was packed with last-minute shoppers, although police said employees were the only ones who witnessed the drama.
Police were called to the drugstore after it was reported a man wielding a large kitchen knife had taken a hostage and demanded drugs from the pharmacist.
An officer called to the scene gave Provencal several warnings to drop the knife and let the hostage go before shooting him in the head.
Provencal was rushed to Foothills Hospital but died later from his injuries.
Police are still investigating the incident, but said it was "very likely" Provencal was looking for a lethal dose of narcotics when he tried to rob the store.
Karen Hala, manager of Alberta Alcohol and Drug Abuse Commission adult services, said for many, a desperate situation can escalate to dangerous levels during an already stressful time of year.

"Often you see (suicidal tendencies) at Christmas time. People are separated from family and they get really suicidal or start thinking about it, so that could be what he was looking for . . . an overdose."
Provencal had recently arrived in Calgary from eastern Canada.
"We found in the business that Christmas is very difficult, whether they're in recovery or whether they're still addicted, they find it an extremely desperate time for them," she said.
Insp. John Middleton-Hope said the officer who shot Provencal joined the force about 2 1/2 years ago.
He has received counselling to help him come to terms with the shooting.

Middleton-Hope said there will be a routine critical incident debriefing this week for the officers involved in the incident, while the professional standards section and the internal affairs investigation unit will work with the homicide unit to complete the investigation.

"Even though a police officer is involved in what appears to be an entirely legitimate shooting of a culprit who was threatening the life of an innocent party, it's still classified as a homicide," he said.
The investigation and review will be conducted in the next couple of weeks.

"I don't think this is easy on anybody and that's one of the reasons we're not disclosing any information on the culprit, we want to be sensitive also to his family . . . they've lost somebody that they cared about."
Kathy Christiansen, program co-ordinator for Alpha House, a drop- in and addictions centre, said Provencal's cry for help came too late.
"It's unfortunate that it got that desperate and that this person didn't get to the point where he was able to get the kind of help he needs."
